column10: Why it is in this deck

A mid-size IT services company taking a new floor. The deck argues desk-sharing from real attendance data, then spends its design budget on daylight and planting. Planting plan and daylight study become mandatory; the acoustic slide stays standard because the ceiling is not exposed.

An operator building a premium centre. Everything is framed as yield — area statement, workstation mix and sellable cabins are mandatory, and community space is a revenue line rather than an amenity. Premium grade pulls in detail junctions and the boardroom. The brand slides drop to optional because a future tenant cannot inherit the client's story.

A captive centre conforming to a parent's global workplace standard. Kit of parts, AV standard, IT infrastructure and security zoning are all mandatory, and the agenda slide is too because the deck will be read asynchronously overseas without a presenter.
C02 raises to M; T02 raises to R

A Series-B company that wants activity-based working. The startup typology strips the deck to its shortest form, but the Collaborative concept pushes back on four slides it would otherwise have cut — settings, workplace model, work styles and booths. That collision is the clearest demonstration of why levels resolve by MAX rather than by last-rule-wins.
